aliases.region: Used as the avatar image of the hoax

description.summary: The 'Momo Challenge' was a 2018-2019 internet hoax and media-driven moral panic alleging that a sinister character named 'Momo' contacted children via WhatsApp and YouTube and instructed them to perform self-harm; investigators, platforms and child-safety organisations found no evidence of any such challenge.
description.full: The Momo Challenge was an internet hoax and moral panic that circulated globally in 2018 and peaked in February-March 2019. It alleged that an entity called 'Momo' — visually represented by a Japanese sculpture of a long-haired, bulging-eyed female figure — contacted children via WhatsApp and embedded videos on YouTube, instructing them to perform self-harm or suicide tasks. The image used was 'Mother Bird', a sculpture by Japanese artist Keisuke Aiso (also reported as Keisuke Aiso of Link Factory), originally exhibited in 2016 and not created in connection with any challenge. Police and child-safety organisations including the NSPCC, Samaritans, the UK Safer Internet Centre and India's Central Bureau of Investigation declared the challenge unfounded. YouTube reported finding no videos showing or promoting any such challenge and demonetised related content. The episode is now widely studied as a textbook moral panic generated by social-media chain warnings and amplified by mainstream media coverage.

etymology.origin: The name 'Momo' was attached online to the 'Mother Bird' sculpture by Japanese artist Keisuke Aiso (Link Factory), exhibited in 2016.
etymology.meaning: An invented internet handle for the avatar image; not connected to a real entity or person.
etymology.first_use: 2018, in early WhatsApp / YouTube chain warnings.

physical.morphology: Not a creature: an artistic sculpture image used as the avatar of an online hoax.

habitat_preference: YouTube comment sections / embedded videos (per chain warnings)
patterns: Spread through chain-warning messages and concerned-parent posts
Amplified by tabloid media and social-media celebrities

range.description: Global, on the English-language internet, with substantial coverage in Latin America, India, Europe and North America.

peak_activity_periods.description: First wave of police warnings (Argentina, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain, Canada, Mexico, USA) and South-American / Indian press coverage
Global peak of the moral panic following Police Service of Northern Ireland warning and Kim Kardashian post; subsequent debunking by NSPCC, Samaritans, YouTube and CBI India

origins.cultural_roots: Internet chain-letter and creepypasta traditions; precursor moral panic of the Blue Whale Challenge.
origins.earliest_accounts: YouTube videos and WhatsApp warnings beginning July 2018.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of a wider lineage of online 'sinister figure contacts your child' chain warnings.

timeline.event: Japanese artist Keisuke Aiso (Link Factory) exhibits the sculpture 'Mother Bird' at Tokyo's vanilla gallery; the sculpture is unrelated to any challenge
timeline.significance: Origin of the image later attached to the hoax

timeline.event: Initial YouTube discussions of an alleged self-harm phenomenon similar to the Blue Whale Challenge
timeline.significance: Earliest online traces of the Momo Challenge narrative

timeline.event: Police forces in Argentina, Germany, Luxembourg, Spain, Canada, Mexico and the USA issue warnings; news reports allege WhatsApp self-harm messages in South America and India
India's Central Bureau of Investigation declares the claims 'far fetched and devoid of any evidence' and notes 'the game has not claimed any victim'
Keisuke Aiso destroys the original 'Mother Bird' sculpture (which had been disintegrating naturally)
timeline.significance: Symbolic end of the image's physical existence

timeline.event: Global moral-panic peak: Police Service of Northern Ireland and Kim Kardashian post public warnings

NSPCC, Samaritans, UK Safer Internet Centre and child-safety experts urge media to stop amplifying the unfounded panic; YouTube reports finding no videos promoting any such challenge and demonetises Momo content

history.modern_era: The Momo Challenge is now widely cited in journalism and media-literacy education as a textbook 21st-century moral panic. The case is also taught in the context of WhatsApp / YouTube content moderation and the role of celebrity and tabloid amplification in spreading unverified online warnings.

physical.name: 'Mother Bird' sculpture
physical.description: The image used as 'Momo' in the hoax is the 'Mother Bird' sculpture by Japanese artist Keisuke Aiso (Link Factory), exhibited in Tokyo's vanilla gallery in 2016. It was unrelated to any 'challenge'.
physical.analysis: The sculpture's origin is well documented; the use of the photograph as the avatar of an alleged self-harm challenge is the hoax overlay.

scientific.name: Moral-panic / mass-hysteria model
scientific.description: Sociologists and child-safety experts characterise the Momo Challenge as a moral panic driven by chain warnings, parental anxiety, social-media virality, and tabloid amplification, in line with established models of mass hysteria.
evidence_cited: Absence of confirmed cases linked to the Challenge
Documented timeline of warnings spreading without verified incidents
Pattern of celebrity and tabloid amplification

skeptical.name: Hoax
skeptical.description: The Momo Challenge as described never existed: there is no evidence of any coordinated content, attacker, or actual harm linked to it.
evidence_cited: YouTube finding no videos showing or promoting any such challenge
CBI India statement (2018-08-29) describing claims as 'far fetched and devoid of any evidence'

stories: Variants of the 'Momo will contact your child' chain warning
folklore.beliefs: The Momo Challenge is a documented hoax; belief in it is best understood as a sociological phenomenon rather than a description of any real entity or activity.

literature: Media-literacy and online-safety case studies citing the Momo Challenge as a moral panic
other: Use of the 'Mother Bird' image in subsequent internet meme culture
Coverage in the Police Service of Northern Ireland 2019 warning and subsequent retractions
